Well yes, but when we use the inference confidence level it means we used inference to come to a conclusion. Here's an example of inference (notice the ``infer()`` call) :
```python
>>> import astroid
>>> a = astroid.extract_node('''
... import argparse
... 
... parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
... parser.add_argument(
...     "config_folder", help="Path to the project configuration folder"
... )
... args = parser.parse_args()
... try:
...     int(args.config_folder) / 0
... except:
...     parser.error(
...         f"Your configuration folder can't be divided by zero, use something else !"
...     )
... ''')
>>> list(a.handlers[0].body[0].value.func.infer())[0]
<BoundMethod error of argparse.ArgumentParser at 0x140506382647696>
```
In this example we can check that the parser.error is argparse parsing and not a call to logging.error.

Some... 

Sometimes we want to iterate over all inference results and just handle the exceptions. For example, for file wrappers the inference is flaky as the `io` module does things we don't understand. However, because we know this we don't want to focus on the flaky total result but focus on the first sub-result as we can determine whether we are looking at an `io` object from it. I know that that is not the best explanation, but I can't think of a better example right now.

That said, if you're looking to contribute checking all `infer()` calls and seeing whether their exception branched are covered would be a good way to start removing some of them. I think there is actually an issue in `astroid` about doing the same there.

_For a future project we could even look at something like `safe_iterating_infer` to catch some but not all exceptions and return an iterator, but that's not something we should look at right now_

Although it runs automatically in CI, all the CI jobs that start on the commit that is then rejected by `pre-commit` (in this case https://github.com/PyCQA/pylint/pull/7520/commits/59feeaeae8fdebacd878b197c8ae6a2c995e98b5) do take up a "runner" and some minutes of our CI. When there are multiple people working on various PRs this can block our CI a bit, especially since the Primer jobs block runners for 30+ min. Running `pre-commit` locally prevents taking up those initial runners.
